summary:
DeRa: AI-Powered Astronaut Health Monitoring
DeRa is a web-based health monitoring and decision-support system for astronauts on long-duration missions. It streams eight vital signs, including heart rate, oxygen saturation, core temperature, HRV and blood pressure, into one mission dashboard with 24-hour trends. A Python Isolation Forest model flags subtle drift in a crew member’s baseline. Each alert comes with an explanation, such as “linked to sleep loss and heavy workload”, so astronauts and flight surgeons can see why it fired.
It addresses the challenge, creating health monitoring software for astronauts, by working where Earth-based support can’t. An offline-first sync engine keeps data safe during deep-space communication delays and uploads it without duplicates when the link returns. Role-based access serves astronauts, flight medical officers, administrators and researchers. Reference ranges are calibrated from NASA OSDR and Twins Study research, and every dataset it labelled as real, simulated or AI-generated.
It matters because on a Mars mission, help is minutes to hours away. Catching small health changes early can keep crews safe and missions on track.
details:
Project name: DeRa - Space Health Monitoring Software | Team Name: Houstan’s Six | Challenge: Create a Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts

What it does and how it works
DeRa is an AI-powered health monitoring and decision-support system for astronauts on long-duration missions. It takes in vitals such as heart rate, blood oxygen, core temperature, heart rate variability and blood pressure from wearable biosensors. Each reading is checked against physiological limits, and impossible values are rejected. A Python machine-learning service (an Isolation Forest of 50 trees) scores each astronaut’s readings against their own personal baseline. When it flags something, the dashboard shows which vitals contributed most and links them to context such as sleep loss or heavy exercise workload. A flight medical officer can then review the alert.

Benefits

  • It catches small changes in health early, before they become emergencies.
  • It keeps working when the link to Earth drops. Data is queued offline and syncs without duplicates once the link returns.
  • Its alerts are explainable rather than a black box.
  • Each role sees only what it needs (astronaut, flight medical officer, mission administrator, researcher).

Intended impact
We want crews travelling to the Moon and Mars to rely less on Earth-based medical support, and to give flight surgeons clear, trustworthy information for fast decisions.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Front end: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, D3, Three.js, Framer Motion.
  • Back end: Node.js and Express, with a JSON database that writes atomically.
  • ML service: pure Python (standard library only).
  • AI assistant: Google Gemini API.
  • Packaging and testing: Docker, plus 103 automated tests in 15 suites.
  • Hardware: designed to ingest data from wearables such as the Zephyr BioHarness 4, a pulse oximeter, a core-temperature sensor and dosimeters. The demo uses simulated telemetry.

How it is creative

  • Built-in mission scenarios let a judge see normal operations, gradual health drift, sensor failure and a deep-space communication blackout.
  • Every number is labelled by origin: real research data, simulated, illustrative, user-entered or AI-generated.
  • The ML service has no external dependencies, so it is light enough to run on board.

Factors we considered

  • Data trust: NASA research (OSDR, the Twins Study, HRP, ISS ThermoLab) sets our reference ranges, and simulated data is always labelled.
  • Sensor errors: bad readings are kept as “possible sensor artifact” instead of being treated as illness.
  • Medical safety: the system shows correlations only and never claims a cause.
  • Connectivity: deep-space delay and outages shaped the offline-first design.
  • Privacy and access: role-based access control, audit logs and separation between astronauts’ data.
  • Reliability: self-healing storage and duplicate prevention
